lead: Drying is not one speed. A wet solid first loses surface water at a steady rate, then slows as water must travel from inside. The drying rate curve plots rate R against moisture X and makes both stages visible. Its shape is measured in a simple batch test: weigh the sample, convert to X, differentiate, divide by drying area. The drying time is (m_s/A) times the area under the 1/R curve between the two moistures, with m_s in kg dry solid and A in m². This is how batch times, dryer capacity and the effect of air conditions are estimated before sizing equipment.
prereq: You need Chapter 7.6 for moisture content X, equilibrium moisture X* and bound and free water.

sections.h3: From weighings to a rate curve

blocks.text: A batch drying test uses a thin sample in air at fixed dry-bulb temperature, humidity and velocity. Record the sample mass m at times t. If m_s is the dry-solid mass, then X = (m − m_s)/m_s kg water per kg dry solid. Plot X against t; the slope dX/dt at each point is negative. The drying rate is R = −(m_s/A)(dX/dt), where A is the exposed drying area in m² and R is kg water evaporated per m² per hour. The dry-solid mass m_s carries units kg dry solid.

items: Dry a known wet sample at constant air conditions.
Weigh it at fixed intervals and compute X at each time.
Draw X against t and find slopes dX/dt.
Multiply by −m_s/A to get R at each X.
Plot R against X; mark the flat part and the fall.

blocks.where: R is drying rate in kg/(m²·h); m_s is dry-solid mass in kg; A is drying area in m²; X is moisture in kg/kg dry solid; t is time in h.

sections.h3: Constant rate, critical point, falling rate

blocks.text: In the constant-rate period the surface is wet. Water evaporates as from a free liquid surface, so R stays at R_c. This ends at the critical moisture X_c, when the surface can no longer supply free water. Below X_c the rate falls. In a simple linear falling-rate stage the rate falls in proportion to the free moisture above X*: R = R_c(X − X*)/(X_c − X*). Here X* is the equilibrium moisture, the value at which drying stops. Many solids show a second, slower diffusion-controlled stage near dryness.

blocks.where: t_c is constant-rate time in h; X₁ is initial moisture; X_c is critical moisture; R_c is constant drying rate; other symbols as before.

blocks.text: t_f = (m_s (X_c − X*)/(A R_c)) ln((X_c − X*)/(X₂ − X*))
blocks.where: t_f is falling-rate time in h; X_c − X* is free moisture at the critical point; R_c is the constant drying rate in kg/(m²·h); A is drying area in m²; m_s is dry-solid mass in kg; X₂ is final moisture above X*; ln is the natural logarithm. Use this for one straight falling line ending at X*.

blocks.text: If X₂ is above X_c, only t_c applies. If X₂ is below X_c, total time is t_c + t_f. For a curved falling stage, integrate graphically: t = (m_s/A) ∫ dX/R from X₂ to X₁, which is the area under the 1/R curve.

Higher air temperature and lower humidity raise R_c and often X_c, because evaporation is faster. Air velocity raises R_c by thinning the boundary layer, but it barely changes the falling-rate period, where internal diffusion controls. Doubling the bed thickness roughly doubles m_s/A and the time, but a thick bed can dry unevenly. Shrinkage reduces A, so the real rate falls faster than the ideal line. Case hardening seals the surface, trapping water inside and adding a slow second falling stage. The measured curve, not a single formula, is the safe basis for design.

items: Constant rate: air temperature, humidity and velocity all matter.
Falling rate: internal diffusion dominates, so velocity matters little.
Thickness sets the mass per area and so the time.
Shrinkage and case hardening bend the real curve away from the ideal.

figure.caption: The rate is flat at 1.5 kg/(m²·h) from X = 0.40 down to the critical X_c = 0.20, then falls in a straight line towards zero at X* = 0.05.

spec.aria: A drying rate curve that is flat at 1.5 from X equal to 0.40 down to the critical 0.20 and then falls to zero at the equilibrium moisture 0.05.

examples.question: A batch dryer holds 50 kg of dry solid with an exposed drying area A = 1 m². The solid is dried from X₁ = 0.40 to X₂ = 0.10 kg/kg dry solid. Tests give X_c = 0.20, X* = 0.05 and R_c = 1.5 kg/(m²·h). Find the constant-rate time, falling-rate time and total drying time.
steps: Dry-solid mass m_s = 50 kg; area A = 1 m²; R_c = 1.5 kg/(m²·h).
Initial moisture X₁ = 0.40 is above X_c = 0.20, so a constant-rate period exists.
Final moisture X₂ = 0.10 is below X_c, so the falling-rate period follows.
For one straight falling line to X* = 0.05: t_f = (m_s (X_c − X*)/(A R_c)) ln((X_c − X*)/(X₂ − X*)).
Total time t = t_c + t_f = 6.67 + 5.49 h = 12.16 h, about 12.2 h.
examples.answer: The constant-rate time is 6.67 h, the falling-rate time is 5.49 h and the total drying time is about 12.2 h.
examples.check:
import math
m_s = 50.0
A = 1.0
R_c = 1.5
X1 = 0.40
Xc = 0.20
X2 = 0.10
Xstar = 0.05
t_c = (m_s/(A*R_c))*(X1-Xc)
t_f = (m_s*(Xc-Xstar)/(A*R_c))*math.log((Xc-Xstar)/(X2-Xstar))
print(f"{t_c:.2f}")
print(f"{t_f:.2f}")
print(f"{t_c+t_f:.1f}")

traps: Using the constant-rate formula below X_c: t_c = (m_s/(A R_c))(X₁ − X_c) stops at X_c, even when X₂ is lower.
Forgetting that R_c is per m² of drying area, not per kg of solid; the factor m_s/A must appear.
Putting X₂ = X* in the log formula divides by zero; the final moisture must be above X*.
Expecting air velocity to speed the falling-rate period; it mainly changes R_c.
Mixing X on a dry basis with wet-basis moisture; these formulas use kg water per kg dry solid.

quiz.a: The moisture content at which the constant-rate period ends and the falling-rate period begins.

quiz.q: Why does the drying rate stay constant at first?
quiz.a: The surface remains wet, so water evaporates as from a free liquid surface and the rate is set by the air conditions.

quiz.q: A solid has m_s/A = 20 kg/m², R_c = 2.0 kg/(m²·h), X₁ = 0.35 and X_c = 0.15. Find the constant-rate time.
Air velocity is doubled during the falling-rate period. What happens to the drying time and why?
quiz.a: The time changes little. The rate is controlled by diffusion of water inside the solid, not by the air boundary layer at the surface.

quiz.q: Why is X* subtracted in the falling-rate driving force?
quiz.a: X* is the equilibrium moisture. No net drying occurs at X*, so the driving force is the free moisture X − X*.

quiz.q: For X_c = 0.20, X* = 0.04, X₂ = 0.09, m_s/A = 30 kg/m² and R_c = 1.2 kg/(m²·h), find the falling-rate time.
A real drying curve shows a sharp second fall near dryness. Give two reasons.
quiz.a: Shrinkage reduces the drying area, and case hardening seals the surface so water diffuses more slowly from inside.

quiz.q: Write the formula for drying rate R from a batch test.
quiz.a: R = −(m_s/A) dX/dt, where m_s is dry-solid mass, A is drying area and X is moisture on a dry basis.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial drying curves are measured for each food, pharmaceutical and ceramic product because shrinkage, cracking and colour set the safe air temperature. Near dryness, a second falling stage can control the batch time, so moisture profiling by MRI or X-ray is used in research. Model predictive control uses the same 1/R integral to adjust air temperature and flow online. Search for drying kinetics, characteristic drying curve and case hardening in food engineering.
